    FLOODING AND PUBLIC HEALTH

    Diseases

    PUBLIC HEALTH ALERT

    El Niño, flooding and disease

    Health guidance from WHO · not an outbreak report

    El Niño can increase the risk of cholera, malaria, dengue fever and other disease outbreaks in Somalia, mainly through flooding, contaminated drinking water, more mosquitoes and displacement into crowded shelters. It does not directly cause infections.

    WHO's 2026 El Niño assessment identifies cholera and other waterborne diseases, malaria, dengue and Rift Valley fever as high or very high risks for Somalia. These are risks to prepare for, not confirmation that any town has an outbreak.

    How flooding raises the risk

    Disease or illnessHow flooding increases the risk
    Cholera and other acute diarrhoeal diseasesFloodwater carries sewage into wells, water tanks and food. Cholera can cause life-threatening dehydration very quickly.
    Dysentery and typhoid feverContaminated food and drinking water spread infection, particularly where toilets overflow or sanitation fails.
    Hepatitis A and EPoor sanitation and contaminated water can spread these liver infections.
    MalariaWater left behind after flooding can create mosquito breeding sites.
    Dengue feverMosquitoes breed in water-filled containers, discarded tyres and other places around homes.
    Rift Valley feverHeavy rainfall can trigger outbreaks involving mosquitoes and livestock. People can become infected through mosquito bites or contact with infected animal blood and tissues.
    Skin and wound infectionsContact with dirty floodwater, especially through cuts, increases infection risk.
    Measles and respiratory infectionsCrowded displacement shelters and interrupted vaccination and healthcare can increase transmission.

    These pathways are described in WHO's flood and emergency health guidance. Rift Valley fever has a particularly strong link with heavy rainfall in East Africa.

    What to do now in flood-affected communities

    • Safe drinking water: use properly treated or boiled water, store it in covered containers, and protect wells from sewage.
    • Early diarrhoea treatment: keep oral rehydration salts (ORS) available. Start ORS promptly and seek urgent treatment for profuse watery diarrhoea.
    • Mosquito protection: use insecticide-treated bed nets, repellents and screens; empty small containers holding stagnant water.
    • Livestock precautions: report unusual animal deaths or repeated miscarriages to veterinary authorities; avoid handling sick or dead animals without protection, and boil or pasteurize milk.
    • Accessible healthcare and vaccination: maintain routine vaccinations and promptly report clusters of diarrhoea or fever.

    Flooding can also worsen malnutrition and existing illnesses by disrupting food supplies, medicines and access to clinics. Young children, pregnant women, older adults and displaced families need particular attention.

    This is health guidance based on WHO publications. It is not an official warning or an outbreak report; follow the Ministry of Health and local health workers.

    Sources

    • WHO: Global Public Health Situation Analysis, El Niño 2026 ↗Lists cholera and other waterborne disease, dengue, malaria and Rift Valley fever as high or very high risks for Somalia (printed page 14).
    • WHO: Somalia Health Emergency Appeal 2025 ↗Describes cholera in Somalia, and malaria and dengue spreading to new districts as a direct result of flooding.
    • WHO: Floods, how to protect your health ↗Explains contaminated drinking water, mosquitoes after floods, and preventing cholera, typhoid and malaria.
    • WHO: Water, sanitation and health in humanitarian emergencies ↗Covers infections linked to poor sanitation: diarrhoeal diseases, dysentery, hepatitis A and E, and skin infections.
    • WHO: Rift Valley fever fact sheet ↗Links outbreaks in East Africa to El Niño heavy rainfall, and explains infection from livestock and mosquitoes and how to prevent it.
    • WHO: Cholera fact sheet ↗Explains contaminated food and water, rapid dehydration, ORS treatment, sanitation and vaccination.

    The first report is the most directly relevant to Somalia and El Niño in 2026. The others explain how these diseases spread and how to prevent them; they do not show that any of these diseases is occurring in a particular town now.

    RECENT OBSERVATIONS · SEPARATE FROM FORECASTS

    Satellite-detected flood water

    Checking latest satellite flood products…
    Select a city or map point to check recent radar observation coverage.

    Satellite classifications show water detected at observation time. They may miss flooding or misclassify water; water can since have moved or receded. Unobserved pixels and transparent areas do not confirm safety. These layers do not measure affected population.

    City marker priority:Purple pins · unverified community reportsLower rainfallRainfall watchElevated rainfall / river watchHigh observed river thresholdData unavailable

    Flood susceptibility is a static terrain-based screening layer. Historical flood-prone areas are separate evidence. Neither shows current inundation or predicted flood depth. Click any map point for its elevation and a SWALIM layer query.

    Daily rainfall

    mm · select a day to explore

    Days 8–14 have greater uncertainty. Rainfall screening is an exploratory indicator; it does not predict inundation or issue an official warning.

    River outlook / GloFAS

    Model grid ≈5 km. The selected river cell may differ from the local channel. Zero modeled discharge does not establish that a city is flood-free. River dates use UTC.

    Observed river level / FAO SWALIM

    Copernicus API observations / radar & optical

    White patches in true-color imagery are often clouds. Brightness alone does not identify water. Check clouds at the location before assessing flooding; Sentinel-1 radar can support inspection when clouds obscure the ground.
    Checking public Copernicus APIs…

    The public catalogue API returns satellite acquisitions. Dated flood classifications come from the separate Copernicus CEMS radar service on the map. Scene-wide cloud cover does not measure cloud directly over this city. Custom processed Sentinel-2 imagery requires Copernicus OAuth credentials on the server.

    Connecting to community reports…
    PRIVATE NOTESSource-linked notes on this deviceOpen local log

    These private, unverified notes are stored in this browser only. They are separate from shared community reports. Add a date and source link for later reference.

    Know what the data can tell you.

    Rainfall screening: lower <10 mm/day; watch 10–24.9 mm/day; elevated ≥25 mm/day. These app-defined thresholds are not calibrated flood probabilities. Local drainage, upstream rain, river levels and exposure determine actual flooding. Missing data are never treated as zero.

    Copernicus Sentinel-2 true-colour imagery supports visual inspection; clouds can obscure water. The supplied true-colour view covers 12 October 2026 and is a dated reference. Its cloudCoverage=100 setting permits cloudy scenes; it does not measure local cloud cover. Sentinel-2 Browser imagery is not an alert feed. Copernicus CEMS Global Flood Monitoring supplies the separate radar flood classification shown on the map. No affected population or inundated area is estimated without evidence.
